newsitem.title: INDIA: India set to deport Charles Sobhraj to France.
newsitem.headline: India set to deport Charles Sobhraj to France.

text.p: Charles Sobhraj walked free on Friday from years in Indian prisons into the arms of immigration officials waiting to deport him to his native France.
Judge Y.S. Jonwal issued his acquittal order after Public Prosecutor B.L. Kalra said the government was dropping all charges relating to a dramatic 1986 jailbreak that earned Sobhraj fame.

In the surreal style that has marked a life glorified in two books, the judge permitted the 52-year-old Sobhraj to conduct a freewheeling, 90-minute news conference with reporters in a dingy New Delhi courtroom before he issued his acquittal order.
"I have no choice. If I had a choice I would stay here," said Sobhraj. "They'll put me on the first flight to Paris. I don't think I'll have any problems in France. I'm a French citizen."

"It's only a matter of when the documents (court order) are handed over, and then he will have to leave India," said an official of India's Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) who did not wish to be identified.
Minutes after the acquittal order, Sobhraj, wearing a sky-blue shirt and his trademark dark glasses and beret, was whisked away by FRRO officials in a blue police van.

It was not immediately clear when he would be put on a plane out of the country. Sobhraj's lawyer Rajan Bakshi said: "They (FRRO) just have to move him to the airport...It's a question of buying the air ticket and boarding the plane."

French officials in Paris confirmed earlier this week that Sobhraj was free to return to France, and added that Paris was prepared to provide him with a laissez-passer facilitating his return once India issued an order to expel him.
A laissez-passer is a one-way document that would allow Sobhraj to be deported back to Paris. The temporary travel document would not allow Sobhraj to enter a third country.

Judge Jonwal's acquittal order said the government feared that Sobhraj, who won release from Delhi's maximum-security Tihar Jail on Monday, would remain at liberty in India if the pending jailbreak case was not resolved speedily.
Only one of 173 prosecution witnesses had been examined in the jailbreak case, Judge Jonwal said, and the government was worried about Sobhraj.

In his order, Jonwal quoted Prosecutor Kalra as saying Sobhraj has a "talent for forgery, self disguise, pharmacology traps, frauds, poisoning and jail escape and that no one is safe from his savage machinations...and his release from jail can be a menace to society and threat to the security of the state."

Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. He has since been charged with a long string of crimes including murder, serving time for some and winning acquittal in others.

Sobhraj, who was born to a French father and a Vietnamese mother, was philosophical about his departure. "I don't like the idea of going to France. I will definitely come back to India. I'm attached emotionally to India. I feel part of India."
Asked if he had any advice for his former jailmates, he said: "Crime does not pay. I have only one piece of advice -- whenever you move out of here, never come back."
Sobhraj said he would now concentrate on working on a $15 million film based on his life.
He said it would be produced in France in English with American actors. He would write the script but would not play the title role.
"Part of the momey I'm going to set aside for my future and my family. With the rest I'm going to build an institution in India where poor children can be educated," he said.
What had he learnt in prison? "Patience," he said.
